title: Applied anatomy: the axilla and brachial plexus

related.why: Median and ulnar nerves in the hand: the distal end of the same plexus
Thoracic inlet: where the lower trunk meets a Pancoast tumour

brief.scenario: A 24-year-old motorcyclist was thrown onto his right shoulder. He cannot lift his arm away from his side or bend his elbow. This is a verbal viva: the examiner will ask you to describe the brachial plexus, and will read out a description of a prosection of the axilla.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the brachial plexus and axilla, including the written description the examiner reads out, and relate them to his injury.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches. Then map his deficit onto the plexus.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Describing the plexus without saying where his lesion is, or whether it is before the ganglion.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Weak abduction and elbow flexion with C5–6 sensory loss is an upper trunk pattern."

flow: Nerve at risk at the shoulder

grid.label: Plexus structure
grid.fail: Cannot give the order roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches, or gives the wrong roots.
grid.pass: Roots C5–T1; upper (C5–6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1) trunks; cords named by their relation to the axillary artery.
grid.high: Adds the five terminal branches and their cords; cords surround the second part of the axillary artery, behind pectoralis minor.

grid.label: Walls of the axilla
grid.fail: Cannot name the walls or the apex.
grid.pass: Anterior: pectoralis major and minor. Posterior: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi. Medial: serratus anterior. Lateral: intertubercular sulcus.
grid.high: Adds the apex (clavicle, first rib, upper border of scapula) as the route from the neck for the plexus and vessels.

grid.label: Contents of the axilla
grid.fail: Names only lymph nodes, or puts the plexus outside the axilla.
grid.pass: Axillary artery and vein, cords and branches of the plexus, lymph nodes and fat.
grid.high: Divides the artery into three parts by pectoralis minor; the axillary sheath wraps artery and plexus.

grid.label: Localises the lesion
grid.fail: Says 'brachial plexus injury' with no level, or blames the axillary nerve alone.
grid.pass: Weak abduction and elbow flexion, C5–6 sensory loss, normal triceps and hand: upper trunk (C5–6), Erb's pattern.
grid.high: Explains why it is not an axillary nerve lesion (biceps and lateral forearm lost too); describes the waiter's tip posture.

grid.label: Pre- or postganglionic
grid.fail: Does not know the difference or why it matters.
grid.pass: Preganglionic is root avulsion from the cord: cannot be repaired directly. Postganglionic may recover or be grafted.
grid.high: Names clues to avulsion: Horner's syndrome, winged scapula, weak rhomboids, raised hemidiaphragm. Each branch leaves near the roots.

grid.label: Axillary nerve
grid.fail: Cannot relate the axillary nerve to the humerus.
grid.pass: Passes through the quadrangular space and winds round the surgical neck; at risk in shoulder dislocation and neck of humerus fracture.
grid.high: Tests deltoid and the regimental badge patch before and after reduction; names the posterior circumflex humeral artery with it.

grid.label: Next steps
grid.fail: Offers physiotherapy and review with no specialist referral.
grid.pass: Documents a full neurological examination and refers early to a specialist brachial plexus service.
grid.high: Adds MRI to look for root avulsion, and says early referral matters because nerve transfer results are time-dependent.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Take me through the brachial plexus.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Roots C5 to T1 form three trunks: upper from C5 and C6, middle from C7, lower from C8 and T1. Each divides into anterior and posterior divisions, which form the lateral, medial and posterior cords, named by their relation to the axillary artery.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the walls of the axilla?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Anterior, pectoralis major and minor. Posterior, subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi. Medial, serratus anterior. Lateral, the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The axillary artery and vein, the cords and branches of the plexus, lymph nodes and fat.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Abduction and elbow flexion are MRC 3. Triceps and the hand are normal. Sensation is reduced over the lateral arm and forearm. Where is the lesion?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The upper trunk, C5 and C6. This is Erb's pattern.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Why does it matter if it's pre- or postganglionic?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A preganglionic injury is a root avulsion from the spinal cord and can't be repaired directly. A postganglionic injury may recover or can be grafted.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Which nerve is at risk at the neck of the humerus?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The axillary nerve. It passes through the quadrangular space and winds round the surgical neck, so it's at risk in dislocation and in fractures there.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd document a full neurological examination and refer him early to a brachial plexus service.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Take me through the brachial plexus.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Roots C5 to T1, upper, middle and lower trunks, divisions, then lateral, medial and posterior cords around the second part of the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor. Musculocutaneous from the lateral cord, ulnar from the medial, median from both, axillary and radial from the posterior.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Four walls, and an apex between the clavicle, first rib and upper border of the scapula. That is where the plexus and vessels enter from the neck.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Pectoralis minor divides the artery into three parts, and the axillary sheath wraps the artery and plexus together.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He has weak abduction and elbow flexion, and C5–6 sensory loss. Could this be the axillary nerve?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No. The axillary nerve doesn't supply biceps or the lateral forearm. This is an upper trunk lesion. At rest you'd expect the waiter's tip posture: arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd look for signs of avulsion from branches that leave near the roots: winging from the long thoracic nerve, weak rhomboids from the dorsal scapular nerve, a raised hemidiaphragm from the phrenic. If T1 is involved, Horner's syndrome.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The axillary nerve at the shoulder?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It runs with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. I'd test deltoid and the regimental badge patch and record them before and after any reduction.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: MRI to look for root avulsion. I'd refer early, because nerve transfer results depend on time since injury.

failures.move: Calling weak abduction and elbow flexion an axillary nerve injury.
failures.consequence: Misses the upper trunk lesion; biceps is not supplied by the axillary nerve.

failures.move: Not asking whether the injury is pre- or postganglionic.
failures.consequence: Misses the question that decides prognosis and surgery.
Every later localisation is built on the wrong map.
Delays specialist assessment in an injury where timing affects the result.

recovery.when: You lose track of the plexus
recovery.line: Let me go back to the roots: five roots, three trunks, six divisions, three cords, five terminal branches.
The muscles that are weak share C5 and C6, and the ones that work don't, so it's the upper trunk.

knowledge.fact: Roots C5–T1. Upper trunk C5–6, middle C7, lower C8–T1. Cords named by relation to the axillary artery.
Upper trunk (Erb's): weak abduction and elbow flexion, waiter's tip posture.
Lower trunk: weak hand intrinsics and clawing; Horner's syndrome if T1 is avulsed.
Preganglionic clues: Horner's, winged scapula, weak rhomboids, raised hemidiaphragm.
Axillary nerve: quadrangular space, surgical neck, deltoid and regimental badge patch.

recall.think: Which trunk, and is it before or after the ganglion?
recall.say: "This is an upper trunk, C5–6, lesion."
do: Map weak muscles and numb skin to roots
recall.trap: Weak abduction is not always the axillary nerve. Check biceps.
recall.finish: Early referral to a brachial plexus service.

partner.opening: This is a verbal viva. Take me through the brachial plexus from roots to branches, then we'll talk about the axilla and the patient.

reveals.finding: Read out: in a prosection of the right axilla, viewed from the front with both pectoral muscles reflected, the back wall is formed, from above down, by a broad muscle lying on the front of the scapula; a thick, rounded muscle passing from the lower part of the scapula towards the humerus; and a broad, flat tendon that curves around the lower border of that rounded muscle to reach the floor of the groove on the front of the humerus. Ask: which muscles form this wall, and what forms the other walls?
Abduction and elbow flexion MRC 3. Triceps, wrist and hand normal. Reduced sensation over the lateral arm and lateral forearm. No ptosis or miosis.
No winging, rhomboids normal, chest X-ray shows a normal diaphragm.

push.question: Take me through the plexus.
push.expect: Roots C5–T1, three trunks, divisions, three cords named around the axillary artery, five terminal branches.

push.question: What are the walls of the axilla?
push.expect: Pectorals; subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi; serratus anterior; intertubercular sulcus. Apex from the neck.

push.question: What does it contain?
push.expect: Artery (three parts), vein, plexus, nodes, fat.

push.question: Where is his lesion?
push.expect: Upper trunk, C5–6. Not the axillary nerve: biceps is weak too.

push.question: Why does pre- or postganglionic matter?
push.expect: Avulsion cannot be repaired directly. Clues: Horner's, winging, rhomboids, diaphragm.

push.question: What happens next?
push.expect: Document, MRI, early referral to a brachial plexus service.

curveballs.prompt: His right eyelid droops and the pupil is small.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Horner's syndrome: T1 sympathetic fibres are damaged near the root. It suggests a preganglionic injury extending to the lower roots, with a poorer outlook.

curveballs.prompt: His scapula wings when he pushes against a wall.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Long thoracic nerve (C5–7) arises from the roots, so its loss points to a preganglionic injury.

curveballs.prompt: Where is the axillary nerve at risk?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Quadrangular space and surgical neck of humerus: dislocation and proximal humeral fracture.
